strengths: The core idea is elegant and practical: apply a Laplace approximation to a single reference model to obtain a conditional score distribution, replacing the need for many shadow models. This is a sensible use of last-layer Bayesian inference (Kristiadi et al.) in a new application area.

The main empirical result (Table 1) is compelling: BMIA with n=1 reference model outperforms LiRA/RMIA/Attack-R with n=8 on most datasets and FPR regimes, at roughly 1/8 the training cost, and also wins under architecture mismatch (Fig. 4) and OOD non-members from CINIC-10 (Table 2).
The evaluation is broad (five datasets, tabular and image, multiple architectures) and follows the standard offline MIA threat model with a stringent data-splitting protocol.

Good ablation coverage: sample size effects, diagonal vs. KFAC vs. full Hessian, marginal-likelihood vs. validation tuning of the prior, MC vs. linearized predictive distributions, and an honest limitations section acknowledging the method may be surpassed when compute is abundant.
The motivating analysis of why quantile regression (QMIA) fails in low-density regions via the aleatoric/epistemic decomposition (Eq. 10, Fig. 1) is a useful framing of the problem.
weaknesses: A mismatch between claims and implementation: the paper motivates BMIA by capturing 'epistemic uncertainty' of the model, but only the last layer is treated probabilistically; the feature extractor's epistemic uncertainty is ignored. Whether last-layer posterior variance actually approximates the reference-model-to-reference-model variability that LiRA empirically estimates is asserted but never directly validated (e.g., no comparison of the estimated conditional distribution against an empirical distribution from multiple reference models).

The theoretical analysis is shaky. Proposition 4.2's proof applies Jensen's inequality to a composite function whose convexity is not established (justified only by an ad hoc 'TPR(z) < 0.5' condition), and the sign bookkeeping appears inconsistent: the displayed proposition on p.5 uses '-Phi^{-1}(alpha) sigma_D' while the appendix proof uses '+', and several inequality steps (e.g., replacing E[sigma_D(z)] by sigma_D and E[1/sigma_S] by 1/E[sigma_S] under a negative coefficient) seem to have reversed inequality directions. As written, the central theoretical claim is not convincingly proven.

Internal numerical inconsistencies undermine confidence in reported results: the introduction claims TPR of 37.5% at 1% FPR on CIFAR-10 with a 64% improvement over Carlini et al., but Table 1 reports 8.87% for CIFAR-10 at 1% FPR; Section 5.2 claims a 64% improvement over LiRA (n=8) on CIFAR-100, while 35.75 vs 23.20 is ~54%; the text says '0.01% and 0.1% FPR' while the table reports 0.1% and 1%. Additionally, no error bars or repeated runs are reported, which matters greatly for TPR estimates at 0.1% FPR.

The t-test treats the sampled scores d_i as i.i.d. Gaussian; the Gaussianity of the hinge-score difference under the posterior is assumed from prior empirical observations rather than tested, and the effect of correlated sampling or small N on the validity of the stated p-value (i.e., FPR calibration) is not examined. Reported FPR-calibration of the attack itself is not shown.
On ImageNet, the headline efficiency/accuracy claim is weaker than suggested: RMIA (n=8) essentially ties BMIA at 0.1% FPR (4.39 vs 4.39), so the advantage is dataset-dependent.

Presentation is rough: multiple typos ('sort-of-the-art', 'per-harness', 'zor-mean', 'Approxiamtion', 'per-harness'), inconsistent notation, and some figures (Fig. 2) are anecdotal single-sample illustrations rather than systematic evidence.

strengths: The core idea is clean and practical: converting a single trained reference model into a Bayesian model via (last-layer) Laplace approximation to obtain a conditional score distribution, avoiding the cost of training many shadow models. This is a natural and somewhat novel use of approximate Bayesian inference in the MIA literature.

Extensive empirical evaluation across five datasets (Texas100, Purchase100, CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet) and multiple architectures, comparing against the strongest recent baselines (LiRA, RMIA, QMIA, Attack-R/P) in the standard offline setting.

Reported results are strong: Table 1 shows BMIA (n=1) beating n=8 baselines on most datasets at low FPR while using ~1/8 the training compute, and the OOD/CINIC-10 experiment (Table 2) and architecture-mismatch study (Figure 4) probe robustness beyond the idealized setting.
The ablations in the appendix (Hessian factorization, prior-precision tuning, MC vs. linearized predictive, sample size) are reasonably thorough and support the design choices.
weaknesses: The central conceptual claim is not validated. The paper argues that Laplace-approximation epistemic uncertainty of one reference model substitutes for the distribution over independently trained models that LiRA/RMIA estimate. But the posterior N(ŵ, Σ) captures parameter uncertainty around a single MAP on a single training subset D, not variability across draws of training data — the very thing that drives conditional score distributions for shadow-model attacks. The paper presents no direct evidence (e.g., comparing the LA-estimated conditional distribution to the empirical cross-model distribution) that these two uncertainties coincide, and the mechanism behind the surprisingly large gains remains unexplained. Notably, only the last layer is made Bayesian, so the captured 'epistemic uncertainty' is quite limited, further weakening the motivating story.

The theoretical analysis is shaky. Proposition 4.2's proof (Appendix A.2) invokes Jensen's inequality and a 'variance decomposition inequality' on quantities whose independence/exchangeability is never established; step (30) implicitly factors an expectation of a ratio without justification, and the key inequality E[Var(Q|z)] < Var(Q) is asserted rather than proven. Moreover, the one-sided t-test on E[d_i]=0 tests a mean shift, not the quantile condition Pr(Q >= tau|x,y) = alpha in Eq. (9), so the link between the p-value threshold and actual FPR calibration is loose and unquantified.

Inconsistencies between claims and tables undermine confidence: the introduction claims '37.5% TPR at 1% FPR ... on CIFAR-10' but the numbers match CIFAR-100 (35.75% vs. LiRA 23.20%); Section 5.2 says '0.01% and 0.1% false positive rates' while Table 1 reports 0.1% and 1%. Such discrepancies in the headline claims are concerning.

Statistical rigor of the evaluation is unclear: no error bars, confidence intervals, or repeated runs over multiple target models are reported, despite TPR being estimated at extremely low FPRs (0.1%) where few examples fall in the tail and variance is large.

The attacker threat model has a potential leakage subtlety: the reference dataset D is 'randomly sampled' from the population, but the paper does not clearly state that D is guaranteed disjoint from the target model's training set S; overlap would invalidate the H0 assumption. Similarly, the assumption that the reference model is exchangeable with the target model under H0 (both trained on disjoint data draws) deserves explicit discussion.

Presentation quality is below bar for a main-track submission: numerous typos ('zor-mean', 'Approxiamtion', 'per-harness', 'KAFC' in Figure 5), H0/H1 labels in Eq. (5) inconsistent with Definition 2.1, and awkward phrasing throughout, which suggests insufficient polishing.

The comparison to QMIA's runtime includes its hyperparameter tuning, while BMIA's own tuning costs (marginal-likelihood optimization, choice of predictive scheme per dataset) are not accounted for symmetrically; no code release is mentioned, which hurts reproducibility given the many implementation choices (KFAC, LLN vs. MC, per-dataset schemes).

strengths: The core idea is simple, well-motivated, and practically valuable: replacing many shadow/reference models with a single reference model plus a Laplace approximation to obtain conditional score distributions is a natural and novel application of Bayesian deep learning to membership inference.

The empirical evaluation is broad and convincing on the main claim: Table 1 covers five datasets, compares against strong recent baselines (LiRA, RMIA, QMIA, Attack-R/P) at matched settings, and reports computation time, showing BMIA often achieves the best TPR at low FPR with roughly 1/8 the training cost.

The paper includes a genuine motivation study (Figure 1 toy experiment, Figure 2 distribution comparison) explaining why conditional attacks and proper variance estimation matter at low FPR, which is pedagogically useful.

Substantial ablation coverage: sample size effects, Hessian factorizations (Diagonal/KFAC/Full), prior tuning via marginal likelihood vs. validation, MC vs. linearized predictive distributions, mismatched reference architectures (Figure 4), and OOD non-members (CINIC-10, Table 2).

Honest limitations discussion acknowledging that BMIA may be outperformed when compute is abundant, and a practical 'offline' attacker setting where the attacker has no access to target training data.
Reasonable reproducibility: the method builds on the public laplace library, and training details, dataset splits, and hyperparameter choices are described in the appendix.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is thin and does not actually distinguish BMIA from other conditional attacks. Propositions 4.1/4.2 assume Gaussian score distributions and show (roughly) that conditional attacks beat marginal attacks, but say nothing about why the Laplace posterior over a single model is a good surrogate for the distribution of independently retrained reference models — the central conceptual leap of the method is asserted, not analyzed or empirically validated (e.g., no comparison of BNN posterior variance vs. shadow-model ensemble variance).

The proof of Proposition 4.2 (Appendix A.2) is questionable: the claimed convexity of Φ only holds for negative arguments (needs TPR(z) < 0.5, which conflates the per-z argument sign with an unverifiable condition), and steps (31) and (33) invoke an undefined 'variance decomposition inequality' relating E[σ_D(z)/σ_S(z)] to σ_D/σ_S that is not established. As written, the proof is not rigorous.

Numerical inconsistencies between claims and Table 1 undermine confidence: the introduction claims TPR of 37.5% at 1% FPR and a 64% improvement over Carlini et al. on CIFAR-10, but Table 1 reports 8.87% for BMIA vs. 8.32% for LiRA (n=8) on CIFAR-10 (a ~6% relative gain); Section 5.2 attributes the 64% figure to CIFAR-100 (35.75 vs. 23.20 is ~54%). These discrepancies need reconciliation.

No statistical rigor around the headline metrics: TPR at 0.1% FPR is extremely sensitive, yet Table 1 reports single numbers with no error bars, no number of target models / repeated trials, and no confidence intervals on the FPR estimate. Given the small absolute differences on some datasets (e.g., Purchase100 0.71 vs. 0.64), it is unclear which comparisons are significant.

The t-test formulation (H0: E[d_i]=0) rests on Gaussianity of hinge scores under posterior sampling, which is assumed rather than verified; the connection between this one-sample test and the formal membership game (Definition 2.1) is loose.

Only the last layer is treated probabilistically, which further weakens the claimed capture of 'epistemic uncertainty' in the model-training sense; the paper's own framing (Eq. 10) motivates full posterior uncertainty, and the gap between last-layer Laplace and true retraining variability is not discussed.

Presentation issues: the text alternates between 'TPR at 0.01% and 0.1% FPR' and '0.1% and 1%', a 64% improvement attributed to two different datasets, typos ('per-harness', 'zor-mean', 'Approxiamtion'), and inconsistent labels (KAFC vs. KFAC). Proposition 4.2's inequality direction and the remark on α > 0.5 need tightening.
No code release is stated, which, combined with the above, reduces reproducibility of the exact headline results.

strengths: The core idea is clean and well-motivated: using a last-layer Laplace approximation on a single reference model to obtain the conditional (per-example) score distribution, replacing the expensive multi-shadow-model paradigm of LiRA/Attack-R/RMIA. The reported efficiency gain (e.g., 1/8 the training cost of LiRA n=8 with better TPR@1% FPR: 35.75% vs ~23% on CIFAR-100) is substantial and practically relevant for privacy auditing.

The variance decomposition into intra-model (posterior) and inter-model (data resampling) variance (Proposition 3.1) is a useful framing that explains what Bayesian sampling can and cannot buy, and naturally yields the MR-BMIA extension. Appendix A.3's linear-regression interpretation—showing posterior sampling matches the leading-order covariance of retrained estimators but not their centers—is a genuinely insightful clarification.

Experiments are extensive and largely convincing: 10 datasets across three modalities, comparisons against 5 attack families, and ablations over posterior-sampling count, Hessian factorization (Diagonal/KFAC/Full), Bayesian inference method (LA vs SWAG, MC Dropout, ensembles), predictive method (MC vs linearized LLN), and hyperparameter tuning. Robustness analyses (CINIC-10 reference data, OOD non-members, architecture mismatch) go beyond the standard offline MIA evaluation.

Honest treatment of limitations: Gaussianity is empirically diagnosed via QQ-plots and t-statistic distributions (Appendix F.1), with a conformal-calibration fallback for heavy-tailed scores; limitations of quantile regression (QMIA) are analyzed with both theory (Eq. 42) and a toy experiment (Fig. 4).
weaknesses: The theory is weaker than claimed. Theorem 3.2 is essentially monotonicity of a Gaussian tail probability under a reduced threshold—an almost immediate corollary of Proposition 3.1 under strong Gaussian assumptions. Proposition B.2's chain of inequalities (steps 31–35) mixes Jensen's inequality and 'variance decomposition inequality' steps that need additional conditions (e.g., boundedness of 1/σ_S(z), sign of Φ^{-1}(α)) and are not rigorously justified; the framing of 'addressing a fundamental gap in the literature' is overstated.

There is a potential calibration concern at the heart of the single-reference attack: under H0, the null distribution of s0 - s̄ includes inter-model variance σ²_inter (the target model is trained on a different dataset than the reference model), but BMIA with K=1 estimates only the intra-model (posterior) variance. This mismatch could miscalibrate FPR at the extreme 0.1% levels where results are reported. The empirical t-statistic check (Fig. 6) is encouraging but limited; the conformal calibration discussed in Appendix F.1 is presented as a suggestion rather than evaluated in the main results.

The assumption Var(s0) = Var(si) = σ² and independence of s0 from reference scores under H0 is an approximation; the target model's score is a fixed realization whose variance across the training draw need not equal the reference posterior variance, especially when architectures or training procedures differ (partially explored only for architecture mismatch).

Presentation issues: the abstract's code URL is incomplete ('available at'); several citations are sloppy (e.g., Laplace approximation cited to a Laplace biography (Hahn, 2005); Nasr et al. 2021 authors/misc 'Songi', 'Carlin'); some recent citations look suspicious (e.g., 'Liu et al., 2026', 'Yi & Li, 2026' with arXiv ID 2601.11314). Impact statement is boilerplate for a paper whose main purpose is enabling stronger privacy attacks—a brief discussion of dual-use considerations would be appropriate.

Novelty is moderate: the contribution is a well-executed application of existing post-hoc Bayesian machinery (last-layer LA, KFAC, mixture LA) to a known problem (conditional MIA), rather than a new methodological development; the theoretical contribution is supporting rather than foundational.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine practical problem: conditional (per-example) MIA thresholds previously required training many reference/shadow models (LiRA, Attack-R), which is computationally prohibitive. The idea of obtaining the conditional score distribution via a Laplace approximation over a single reference model is sensible, well-motivated, and yields large efficiency gains (Table 1 shows ~1/8 the training cost of LiRA with higher TPR at 0.1%/1% FPR across 10 datasets in three modalities).

The variance decomposition in Proposition 3.1 (intra- vs. inter-model variance, Law of Total Variance) and the monotonicity result in Theorem 3.2 give a clean, if simple, explanation for why Bayesian sampling helps and why multiple references still add value. The linear-regression interpretation in Appendix A.3 is a nice touch that honestly clarifies what posterior sampling does and does not capture relative to retraining.

The experimental evaluation is extensive and largely follows established evaluation protocols (TPR@low FPR, population-level data splits, QMIA-style validation): 10 datasets spanning image, tabular, and text; comparisons against Attack-P/R, LiRA, RMIA, and QMIA; ablations over sample size, Hessian factorization, Bayesian inference method (ensembles, SWAG, MC Dropout); and robustness studies covering distribution shift (CINIC-10 reference), OOD queries, and architecture mismatch — all practically relevant scenarios.

The appendices provide useful diagnostics (normality QQ-plots of hinge scores and t-statistics, Figure 5/6), a calibrated-fallback discussion for non-Gaussian scores, and detailed complexity analysis of the last-layer Laplace approximation, aiding reproducibility. Code is stated to be released.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is modest. Proposition 3.1 is a direct application of the Law of Total Variance, and Theorem 3.2 (power increases in M given a lower threshold) is essentially immediate once variances shrink; it abstracts away the fact that both the null and alternative distributions change and that variance estimates themselves are noisy. Proposition B.2's Gaussian/Jensen argument requires assumptions (convexity region, identical sigma_S across z) that limit its force. The 'provable' framing in the abstract oversells fairly standard analysis.

The method's strength depends heavily on the quality of the Laplace approximation, yet only the last layer is treated probabilistically — meaning the 'intra-model variance' captured is only last-layer epistemic uncertainty, not the full training-run variability that shadow models exhibit. The paper does not deeply analyze when this gap matters (e.g., models where memorization is driven by early-layer or optimization effects), which weakens the claimed generality of the variance-reduction story.

Some experimental comparisons raise fairness concerns: Attack-R/LiRA/RMIA are run with 2–8 references in Table 1 while the claimed 54% improvement over LiRA is against n=8, and the time column omits the LA/Hessian construction and sampling overhead for BMIA (Figure 1c partially addresses this, but a unified end-to-end accounting including storage and Hessian accumulation cost would be more convincing). QMIA's cost note is relegated to a footnote rather than analyzed in the main text.

The t-test relies on Gaussianity of hinge scores and independence assumptions (e.g., 'covariance term is zero' in Appendix A.1 presumes the target sample is a non-member under H0, but the same statistic is used under H1 where this fails). Diagnostics are shown only for selected samples and datasets; a study of mis-calibration rates (empirical FPR vs. nominal alpha) across all settings would substantially strengthen the hypothesis-testing claims.

Novelty is incremental: the paper is essentially a careful combination of known components (last-layer Laplace/KFAC, hinge score from LiRA, Welch–Satterthwaite t-test) applied to a known attack formulation. The conceptual framing (BNN posterior as a cheap substitute for shadow-model retraining) is the main new insight.

The threat model assumes the attacker knows the target architecture and training data distribution and can train a reference model on disjoint data from the same population — reasonable for auditing, but the paper could be clearer that results degrade when these assumptions fail, beyond the preliminary CINIC-10 and mismatch experiments.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated angle: the paper connects Bayesian deep learning (Laplace approximation) to conditional membership inference attacks, offering a principled way to obtain per-instance score distributions from a single reference model, in contrast to the expensive multi-reference approach of LiRA/Attack-R.

The variance decomposition framework (Proposition 3.1, based on the law of total variance) cleanly explains why posterior sampling helps (reduces the dataset-resampling variance contribution) and why gains diminish with more reference models; the linear-regression interpretation in Appendix A.3 is an honest and useful discussion of what posterior sampling does and does not capture.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three modalities (image, tabular, text; 10 datasets) with TPR@low-FPR as the metric, showing consistent improvements over Attack-R, LiRA, RMIA, and QMIA at substantially lower cost (e.g., 54% TPR improvement over LiRA(n=8) on CIFAR-100 at 1/8 the cost).

Thorough ablations: sample size M, Hessian factorization (diagonal vs. KFAC vs. full), Bayesian inference alternatives (SWAG, MC Dropout, ensembles), prior tuning, and predictive-distribution approximations (LLN vs. MC), plus robustness studies for OOD non-members, reference-data mismatch, and architecture mismatch.

Good reproducibility: implementation code is released, training details, accuracy tables, hardware, and complexity analysis of the last-layer Laplace (Appendix G) are provided; empirical diagnostics (Figures 5-6) support the Gaussian/t-test assumptions.

The MR-BMIA extension (mixture Laplace with Welch-Satterthwaite degrees of freedom) is a natural and well-executed instantiation of the theory, and Table 7 shows the expected diminishing returns with growing K.
weaknesses: The theoretical contributions are somewhat incremental: Proposition 3.1 is a direct application of the law of total variance, and Theorem 3.2 follows trivially from monotonicity of the threshold in the variance. Proposition B.2 relies on Gaussian score assumptions and Jensen's inequality under a TPR<0.5 condition, which limits its generality despite being presented as a key result.

Several strong assumptions are not fully justified: the hinge score is assumed Gaussian under the posterior (empirically checked only on selected samples), the target score s0 is assumed to have the same variance as reference scores (Eq. 10), and posterior samples from one reference dataset are treated as exchangeable with scores from independently retrained models. Appendix A.3 acknowledges the center-gap issue, but the practical impact on FPR calibration at very low thresholds (0.1%) deserves more direct empirical validation.

Only last-layer Laplace approximation is used; the claimed epistemic uncertainty quantification therefore covers only the final linear layer. While the ablations partially mitigate this concern, the gap between the conceptual story (full Bayesian posterior) and the implementation is not deeply probed (e.g., when would last-layer uncertainty be insufficient?).

Baselines at n=2,4,8 are trained on halves of a 40% reference population, and the authors' method uses a reference model trained on the same protocol; minor protocol asymmetries (e.g., per-model data quantity, hyperparameter tuning effort for baselines like QMIA, deferred to Appendix D) could affect the strictness of the SOTA comparison.

Some presentation issues: the claim in Theorem 3.2 that power strictly increases with M is proven only under the t-distribution null approximation and Gaussianity; the abstract's 'provably increasing attack power' phrasing is stronger than what the assumptions support.
